# Automation & Workforce Transition Roadmap
## Distribution Network — 5 Regional DCs
### Seven-year program · four capital waves · two deep-automation sites · zero automation-driven involuntary separations

---

## 0. How to read this document

**Numbers convention.** Every quantity here is **illustrative placeholder data** built out from the baseline in §1 to make the logic testable. No figure is sourced from your operation. The deliverable is the *structure*: the sequencing logic, the gates, the guardrails, the transition mechanics, and the measurement system. Anything that must be rebuilt with real data before capital is released is marked **⟨REBUILD IN WAVE 0⟩**.

**What this document decides:**
1. How much automation each site gets, and of what *type* (§4)
2. In what order, and what must be true before each step (§5, §9)
3. How ~430 affected positions are handled without an automation layoff (§6, §7)
4. How service holds through cutover, including for the two accounts already on probation (§8)
5. How we prove — to Finance, not to Engineering — whether returns are real (§10)

**What it refuses to do:** endorse the vendors' 3-year payback (§11), automate before the footprint is settled (§3.4), or announce anything at the anchor site before the plan can be honored (§12).

---

## 1. Baseline ⟨REBUILD IN WAVE 0⟩

### 1.1 Network

| Item | Illustrative value | Definition to lock in Wave 0 |
|---|---|---|
| Regular hourly associates | 1,150 across 5 DCs | FT / PT counted separately; agency excluded |
| Agency temps | ~110 FTE-equivalents | Peak-adjusted average; markup identified separately |
| Salaried | 180 | Ops, IT, HR, maintenance, engineering |
| Blended fully-loaded hourly cost | $25.00/hr regular; $28.00/hr agency | Wage + benefits + taxes + OT premium + markup |
| Annual hourly labor | ~$63.7M | Regular $57.5M + agency $6.2M |
| Turnover (regular) | 33% network (≈380 exits/yr) | Split voluntary / involuntary / temp-conversion, by role, by site |
| Defect rate | 380 per 10,000 shipped lines (3.8‰) | **Per line.** Also report per order (~1.7%) and per shipment. Categories: wrong item, wrong qty, damage, mislabel, short-ship |
| Quality cost | $4.1M/yr | Chargebacks + credits + expedite freight + return freight + rework labor |
| **Revenue at risk** | **$96M/yr across two top-10 accounts on service probation (~11% of revenue; ~$14M gross margin)** | Cure periods, exit rights, rebid dates |
| Capital envelope | $120M over 7 years, ≤$45M in any single year | Confirm with Treasury; confirm covenant headroom |

**The last two rows govern the program.** ~$14M/yr of gross margin is at risk *now*; that is more than any single year of automation labor savings. The first job is not cost reduction. It is to stop losing the accounts — and that job needs almost no capital and cannot wait for robots.

### 1.2 Sites ⟨REBUILD IN WAVE 0⟩

| | **DC-A "Anchor"** | **DC-B** | **DC-C** | **DC-D** | **DC-E** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Regular hourly | 420 | 260 | 190 | 160 | 120 |
| Agency (FTE-eq) | 20 | 45 | 25 | 15 | 5 |
| Turnover | 22% | 48% | 41% | 30% | 28% |
| Avg tenure | 9.2 yr | 2.4 yr | 3.1 yr | 5.8 yr | 6.4 yr |
| Share of town employment | **~11% of local jobs — largest employer** | <0.5% | <0.5% | ~1.5% | <0.5% |
| Building | Owned, 1988, 26 ft clear, 40'×40' grid, uneven floor | Owned, 2015, 36 ft clear, 50'×50', FM-compliant | **Leased, expires Month 34** | Leased through Month 108 | Owned, small, 24 ft clear |
| Volume profile | 55% each-pick, 30% case, 15% pallet | 80% each-pick, high SKU count | 70% each-pick | 40% each / 45% case / 15% pallet | Specialty, low volume, high touch |
| Share of network lines | 34% | 25% | 17% | 15% | 9% |
| Probation accounts served | 15% of their volume | **50%** | **35%** | — | — |
| Local labor market | Loose (few alternatives) | **Very tight** | Tight | Moderate | Moderate |
| Defects per 10k lines | 340 | **480** | 430 | 300 | 260 |

Two facts jump out of this table and set the whole sequence:

- **The site with the worst quality, the worst turnover, the tightest labor market, the best building, and half the at-risk revenue is DC-B — not the anchor.** DC-B is where automation both pays best and hurts least.
- **The site with the most people, the longest tenure, the deepest community exposure, and the worst building for automation is DC-A.** It goes last, on purpose, after the model is proven and the commitments can be made honestly.

---

## 2. Strategic thesis — five judgments that drive everything

**1. Turnover is the transition mechanism, but only site-by-site and role-by-role.**
Network attrition (~380/yr) against an end-state net reduction of ~310 regular positions over seven years looks comfortable **in aggregate, and the aggregate is misleading.** Automation removes roles in step functions: one goods-to-person go-live can retire 110–130 pick/pack positions at one site inside 18 months, while attrition *in those roles at that site* may run 85–110/yr — and you still need most of those people during dual-run. The governing artifact is not a network average but the **site × role × quarter attrition-vs-reduction grid** (§7.1). Until that grid balances for a site, that site's conversion is not approved. Where it cannot balance, the gap is closed with pre-priced flex-ratio reduction, cross-site transfer, and voluntary windows — planned, not improvised.

**2. Automation probably displaces the roles you cannot keep filled — but that is a hypothesis with a named Plan B.**
Working assumption: turnover concentrates in entry-level each-pick and pack, while long-tenured associates hold lead, inventory, receiving, and specialty roles. **Test this in Week 2** with a tenure × role × site crosstab.
- *If confirmed:* the tenured workforce becomes the exception-handling, training, and quality bench — the capability automation cannot buy — and DC-A's tenure profile becomes an asset, not an obstacle.
- *If tenure is concentrated in pick/pack (Plan B):* the problem is materially larger and three things change. (a) DC-A drops from Tier 3 to Tier 2 — relocatable AMR/assist technology, no permanent fixed asset. (b) The transition window extends from 7 to 9–10 years so reductions ride natural retirement. (c) The workforce fund roughly doubles and is front-loaded into a voluntary separation / early-retirement window opened **before** any automation announcement, so departures are self-selected rather than displacement-driven.
This is a Gate-1 board decision, not a staff assumption.

**3. The competitor's failure is now two separate problems: an engineering problem and a change-management fact.**
Public automation failures typically share six features: big-bang cutover; dirty master data (dimensions, weight, cube); no manual fallback; a simultaneous WMS change; go-live inside peak; an under-resourced maintenance function. That is a *plausible hypothesis, not a finding* — so Wave 0 commissions a real teardown (public filings and transcripts, trade-press reconstruction, structured reference calls with the same vendors' *unsuccessful* accounts, site visits where obtainable, targeted hiring of two or three people who lived it) and **publishes it internally, including what contradicts our hypothesis.** Guardrails G4–G9 exist to insure against these modes specifically.
Separately: your associates have read the coverage. Fear is already priced into the building. **Name it in the first all-hands** — "you've seen the story; here is what went wrong there, here is what we're doing differently, and here is what we will tell you if it starts going wrong here" — do not manage around it.

**4. Footprint decisions precede fixed-automation decisions.**
Installing a $40M+ fixed system into a building you should exit, or into a network shape you should consolidate, is the least recoverable error available. DC-C's lease expires in Month 34. Lease terms, building fit (clear height, column grid, floor flatness, power, sprinkler/FM Global rules for high-density storage), permitting, and the automate-vs-consolidate-vs-relocate question are **Wave 0 gates ahead of Wave 1 capital**, not Wave 2 discoveries.

**5. Quality is a process problem before it is a robot problem.**
480 defects per 10,000 lines at DC-B is not primarily a human-accuracy ceiling; it is slotting chaos, unverified master data, missing scan-verification steps, unmanaged training-to-competency, and a temp ratio near 20%. Expect **50–65% of the defect reduction to come from Wave 0 process work at ~2% of the program's capital.** Automation then locks the gain in and takes the rest. Sequencing quality first also buys the political license for everything that follows: the accounts calm down, the board sees delivery, and associates see that the first move was to fix the job, not to replace it.

**Therefore the sequence is:** fix quality and process first (no MHE capital, immediate customer benefit) → prove the automation model at the high-turnover, best-building, tight-labor site → resolve the footprint → deploy deep automation at the anchor site last, when the design is de-risked, the track record is real, and the community commitment can be made honestly.

---

## 3. What we are explicitly *not* doing

| Not doing | Why |
|---|---|
| Lights-out / fully automated DC | No proven each-pick robotics maturity at our SKU breadth; eliminates the fallback that keeps customers |
| Big-bang cutover anywhere | The single most common failure mode in the public record |
| Simultaneous WMS replacement + MHE install | Doubles
